A few words before we start 2026/11/14

> These days it feels like teaching material is mostly read by AI, and AI probably already knows all of this\
> If AI helps with quantization and deployment, do humans — the bottleneck — still need to understand it? I don't know, but right now I want to write down what I've learned from experience\
> Anyway, this course is written for humans, assuming anyone still wants to understand ...

Use PyTorch 2 Export (PT2E) to quantize a model to int8 and other low-bit integers: start from the graph you get out of `torch.export`, see how the quantizer annotates it, how observers are inserted,
what the graph looks like after convert, and finally hand it to a backend such as XNNPACK or ONNX Runtime.

This course targets edge devices with limited compute and power (for example always-on sensing and voice wake-up): small models, a fully integer graph (mostly int8), fixed shapes, and a limited set of ops supported by the backend.
Weight-only int4 and KV-cache quantization, as commonly used for LLMs, are out of scope.

Each module starts with an **overview** that states the questions the chapter answers and its core concepts; the notebooks that follow verify them hands-on, one by one.
All notebook outputs have already been run, so you can read the results directly; to change parameters and rerun yourself, see "Run on your own machine" below.

## The storyline: two parts

M00 is the common foundation: capture the model as a graph and learn to edit it. After that the course splits into two parts, divided by the **Q/DQ graph** produced by `convert_pt2e`:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
    F["fp32 model"] --> P1["Part 1: M01–M06<br/>export → prepare<br/>→ calibrate or train → convert"]
    P1 --> QDQ["Q/DQ graph<br/>fp32 ops simulating int8"]
    QDQ --> P2["Part 2: M07–M10<br/>recognize dq → op → q<br/>swap in int8 kernels"]
    P2 --> D["Runs on device<br/>.pte / .onnx / custom hardware"]
    P2 -. "Quantizer, op list, constraints" .-> P1
```

| | Part 1 | Part 2 |
|---|---|---|
| Chapters | M01–M06 | M07–M10 |
| Starting point | A trained fp32 model | The Q/DQ graph |
| End point | The Q/DQ graph, and its accuracy | An int8 model running on the device |
| Questions answered | Where to quantize, what the scales are, what to do with QAT when PTQ is not enough | Who swaps the units for int8 kernels, what to do when a swap is impossible, how to verify numerics and speed |
| Overview | [Part 1 overview](part1_overview.qmd) | [Part 2 overview](part2_overview.qmd) |

The reading order is Part 1 → Part 2, but the dashed line in the diagram points the other way: the Quantizer is designed around the backend's own kernels (M03),
so in practice you **pick the backend first, then quantize** (the M07 overview, "Before Quantizing, Choose the Backend").
M03 reads and writes a Quantizer from the user's point of view; M10 takes the backend's point of view and writes hardware constraints into a Quantizer.
The Quantizer is the contract between the two parts.

## Two roles: the algorithm engineer and the backend deployment engineer

In practice the two parts are often owned by two kinds of people. One person may play both roles, but what gets handed over is the same.

| | Algorithm engineer | Backend deployment engineer |
|---|---|---|
| Responsible for | Modeling, training, quantization | Choosing the platform, providing the Quantizer, lowering, verification, and deployment |
| Main chapters | Part 1 (M01–M06) | Part 2 (M07–M10) |
| Hands to the other side | Q/DQ graph, fp32 model, data, accuracy report | Quantizer, op list, hardware constraints |
| Owns which numbers | Q/DQ graph vs fp32 | Device output vs Q/DQ graph |

### The order of collaboration

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Algorithm engineer
    participant B as Backend deployment engineer
    B->>A: Quantizer, op list, shape and bit-width constraints
    A->>A: Design and train the fp32 model, avoiding ops outside the list
    A->>A: PTQ or QAT, confirm accuracy on the Q/DQ graph
    A->>B: Q/DQ graph, fp32 model, data, accuracy report
    B->>B: Compliance check, lowering, fallback report
    B->>B: Numerics and speed verification
    B-->>A: Report ops that fell back, accuracy gap, speed
    A->>B: Revised Q/DQ graph
```

The last two steps usually go back and forth several times. The details of each handoff checklist are in the "Role" section of each part overview.

### Four things this division of labor must add

| Easy to miss | Why | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Give the backend information before the model is designed | The op list determines how many segments the graph is split into; you can avoid that when choosing the architecture | M10-3 |
| Handing over only the Q/DQ graph is not enough | The backend needs the fp32 model as a baseline and data to rerun evaluation; some routes also need to convert again | M07 overview, M08-2 |
| QAT consistency is a joint responsibility | The QAT config from the backend must pass the "training graph = convert graph" check | M06-3 |
| When accuracy drops, measure by segment before deciding who investigates | The loss splits into two segments, each owned by one role (see the next section) | M05, M07-1 |

### Accuracy dropped: which segment to check first

Between fp32 and the device sits the Q/DQ graph. Running three versions on the same evaluation data splits the accuracy loss into two segments:

```text
fp32 model
  → Q/DQ graph        Segment 1: loss caused by quantization itself (algorithm engineer)
  → model on device   Segment 2: differences from lowering and integer kernels (backend deployment engineer)
```

Segment 1 can be measured inside PyTorch (M05, M06); segment 2 can only be measured once the backend runs the graph on the device.
Here are three hypothetical accuracy sets showing how to decide:

| fp32 | Q/DQ graph | Device | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| 90% | 82% | 82% | Segment 1 already lost it: the device is just faithfully reproducing the Q/DQ graph; go back and change the quantization config or the model |
| 90% | 89.5% | 82% | Only segment 2 lost it: the Q/DQ graph is fine; investigate lowering or the backend kernels |
| 90% | 89.5% | 89.4% | Both segments are fine: the small gap between device and Q/DQ graph is integer rounding |

In the first case, no amount of backend tuning will recover it; in the second, more QAT by the algorithm engineer won't help.
Split by segment first, so neither side wastes effort. The "small gap" in the last row means the device and Q/DQ graph outputs differ by only 1–2 output LSBs (measured in M08 and M09).

## Run on your own machine

The environment is managed with [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) (Python 3.12). graphviz subgraphs need the system `dot` executable.

```bash
brew install graphviz          # Ubuntu: sudo apt install graphviz
uv sync
uv run jupyter lab             # or open the .ipynb in VS Code and pick .venv as the kernel
```
